sources.locator: Python Packaging User Guide; accessed 2026-07; Virtual Environments, Writing pyproject.toml, Packaging Projects, and Command-Line Tools guides; atomic topic: Project metadata and command entry
sources.claim: pyproject.toml records build-system requirements and project metadata, while a conventional source/test layout and declared command entry point make a package buildable and invocable reproducibly.

canonicalExplanation.summary: `pyproject.toml` is your project's **ID card**: it names the **build backend**, the project's name, version and dependencies, and any **console scripts** — commands like `notes` that call `package.cli:main`. With a `src/` layout, you must install the project (`pip install -e .`) before running it, which proves the package really installs — not just that it works from your folder.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
You've built a note-taking CLI across several modules. Right now you run it with `python src/notes/cli.py` from one exact folder. You want teammates to type `notes add "buy milk"` from anywhere. A src-layout project declares its build backend, project name, version and dependencies, and a console script that calls package.cli:main. In this lesson you'll package and invoke a multi-module command-line application reproducibly.

```predict
{"question": "In pyproject, `notes = \"notes.cli:main\"` under `[project.scripts]` means:", "options": ["Run the file notes.cli", "Create a `notes` command that imports notes.cli and calls main()"], "answer": 1, "why": "`module:function` — installing creates a small launcher that imports the module and calls the function."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Function contracts and returns**, **Interpreter and environment**, **Virtual environments and dependencies**, and **Scripts, indentation and main guard**.

sections.heading: The model: metadata, build backend, entry point
sections.body:
```text
notes-app/
├── pyproject.toml
└── src/
    └── notes/
        ├── __init__.py
        ├── store.py
        └── cli.py        # def main(): ...
```

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=68"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "notes-app"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = ["rich>=13"]

[project.scripts]
notes = "notes.cli:main"
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why use a `src/` folder instead of putting `notes/` at the top?", "answer": "With src layout, `import notes` only works after installation, so your tests check the **installed** package, not a lucky local import."}
```

sections.heading: Install and run
sections.body:
```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .
notes add "buy milk"
```

```predict
{"question": "Does a pyproject.toml pin the exact version of every dependency?", "options": ["Yes, automatically", "No — it declares allowed ranges; a lock file or requirements pin exact versions"], "answer": 1, "why": "`rich>=13` allows many versions. For identical rebuilds, record pinned versions separately (e.g. `pip freeze` or a lock tool)."}
```

examples.title: A src-layout project with a console command
examples.situation: A src-layout project declares its build backend, project name/version/dependencies, and a console script that calls package.cli:main.
walkthrough: **Build backend:** `[build-system]` declares setuptools as the backend that turns the source into an installable wheel.
**Console script:** `notes = "notes.cli:main"`; after `pip install -e .`, running `notes` calls package.cli:main.
examples.result: Teammates install once and run `notes` from any folder, with dependencies installed automatically.

examples.title: The wheel that was missing a module
examples.situation: A project with a flat layout works when run from its folder, but after building a wheel and installing elsewhere, `import notes.store` fails.
walkthrough: From the folder, Python imported files straight from the working tree, hiding the problem.
Package discovery didn't include `store.py` in the built wheel.
Fix: switch to src layout (or configure discovery), install the build in a clean venv, and run the command there.
examples.result: Testing the installed package, not the working tree, catches missing modules before users do.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Adding any pyproject.toml automatically discovers every module, locks all dependencies, and proves the built wheel contains the working tree.
misconceptions.correction: pyproject declares metadata and allowed dependency ranges; discovery depends on layout and configuration, and exact pins need a lock file. Only installing and running the built package in a clean environment proves it works.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The wheel that was missing a module", why did running from the folder hide the bug?

analogy.example: pyproject.toml is like a **shipping label plus packing instructions**: what's in the box, who built it, what else must arrive with it, and which button starts it. A src layout is sealing the box before testing — you test what the customer receives.
usefulFor: testing the installed box, not the workbench
limitations: A label doesn't guarantee contents — you still need to inspect the box (install and test).
Dependency ranges are like "any brand of batteries", not an exact model.

recap.summary: To package and invoke a multi-module command-line application reproducibly, declare the build backend, metadata, dependencies and a console script in pyproject.toml, use src layout, install into a clean venv, and run the command from anywhere. Pin exact versions separately.
